claims.statement: The Axum fallback is subject to the configured proxy concurrency limit, while the local GET /health and GET /metrics routes bypass that limit.

The fallback generates a fresh req_ identifier for the proxy span and locally generated request errors; it is not inserted as an outbound or client-facing HTTP header by the proxy. Provider preparation handles upstream credentials rather than authenticating callers in the fallback handler.

An outbound send retains the inbound method and appends its path and query to the configured upstream base; initial header copying preserves repeated values but removes the fixed hop-by-hop list, Host and Content-Length so the outbound HTTP client can derive host and body framing.

Both providers receive requests only after bounded inbound body buffering with an inclusive 10 MiB cap; a read or size-limit failure returns 400, as does a JSON parse failure when the provider needs JSON.

Without [oauth], passthrough applies configured header replacements except Authorization, forwards opaque original body bytes, and returns no account ID. When [oauth] is present the service chooses the OAuth provider and ignores static [[headers]].

The body-aware OAuth path parses JSON once and starts each provider preparation from copies of the original parsed JSON and filtered headers; the mutated request is serialized for the current account without carrying mutations into later account attempts.

OAuth preparation selects a pool credential, removes client Authorization and x-api-key, injects a Bearer token, merges beta flags, and applies compatibility header and system prompt mutations before returning an account ID.

The proxy consults the provider classifier only for 4xx or 5xx responses associated with an account ID. It buffers the body with bytes() outside the initial-response deadline and without the streaming idle wrapper, substituting empty bytes if buffering fails.
Only a case-insensitive subscription-quota phrase match in an OAuth HTTP 429 triggers cooldown for the configured duration and another account preparation if budget remains.

OAuth classifies 401 and 403 as permanent, disables the selected account, and returns the upstream error without failover. Other classified errors such as a generic 429 or 5xx are returned without retry, failover, or a pool change despite the Transient label.

The outer account-attempt budget is fixed when ProxyState is built: one in passthrough, or the OAuth startup account ID count clamped to at least one, taking IDs from configured providers or the credential store. Admin enrollment modifies the live pool without recalculating that budget.

The handler tracks no tried-account set across quota attempts; each OAuth preparation uses the pool's current round-robin scan, which skips unavailable accounts, restores accounts with expired cooldowns, and can refresh near-expiry credentials inline before the send deadline begins. Distinct account IDs per request are not guaranteed.

A quota response on the final allowed account attempt is returned as the buffered upstream 429. A failed preparation, including failed selection after an earlier quota response, instead returns a proxy 503 rather than the prior 429; it has the same public proxy_error envelope as other preparation failures, not a dedicated pool_exhausted HTTP error type.

The shared upstream client's fixed five-second connect timeout is distinct from the proxy send deadline. A reqwest send error that arrives before the outer timer, even an error due to the client's connect timeout, returns proxy 502 without an explicit retry.

An elapsed Tokio deadline around req.send() permits up to two same-preparation retries at fixed 100 ms intervals, with a fresh timeout per send through status and headers; the third elapsed deadline produces proxy 504. The prepared credentials and body are replayed without account reselection or an idempotent-method check.

Proxy-generated body validation, send, timeout, and preparation failures use a JSON proxy_error type with a message and request ID, while forwarded upstream responses preserve their status and copy response headers except for the fixed hop-by-hop list. An upstream error is not identified solely by its numeric status.

Non-classified responses, including successful SSE and passthrough HTTP errors, stream upstream bytes rather than buffering for classification. Each successful chunk resets the idle deadline; idle expiry logs a warning and sends EOF after the original headers, without a new status, error event or replay, whereas a body transport error is propagated.

The positive [proxy].timeout_secs setting supplies both the per-send initial-response deadline and the idle window for streamed bodies. It defaults to 180 seconds, matches the committed Kubernetes config, and does not cap the total lifetime of an active stream.

For streamed responses the duration metric and in-flight guard track the handler through response return rather than body completion, so a successful HTTP status metric can coexist with a later idle-timeout warning.

The upstream error counter labels a proxy send failure connection and an exhausted initial-response deadline timeout. Pool quota telemetry counts pool_failovers_total before checking the remaining budget, so the count does not establish that another account was reached.
